title: People and cooperations
text:
People and cooperations
The project WetFlorVegChange was conceived by a team of Central European scientists, based primarily at Masaryk University (Core team). However, because one of the main goals of this project is to build a European network of wetland‑vegetation ecologists and to assemble all existing vegetation‑plot time series of inland wetland habitats into the ReSurveyWetlands database, the project relies on the collaboration of numerous experts across Europe (Data contributors).

title: More about the project
text:
In order to provide a comprehensive assessment of floristic and vegetation changes in both managed and unmanaged European wetlands over the last century, the project is divided into four working packages:


This WP aims to establish a European network of wetland vegetation ecologists and gather most of the existing resurveyed plots and vegetation-plot time series of inland wetland vegetation (including eu- and mesotrophic aquatic, marsh, spring, peatland, annual temporary pond, oligotrophic water vegetation, and wet meadows). We will create a common repository for new wetland resurveys and related information, ReSurveyWetlands. This database will eventually be integrated into the ReSurveyEurope database (https://euroveg.org/resurvey/), according to the consensus of data contributors.



The goal of this working package is to explore the trends in floristic and vegetation changes across European wetlands over the past 30 years. The geographic scope will encompass Europe, excluding the Nordic Countries, Russia, and Belarus due to insufficient data.
We aim to answer the following questions:
a) Which wetland vegetation types and habitats are most impacted by floristic and vegetation changes?
b) How do trends in wetlands vary across different European regions?
c) Do wetlands in Central European countries tend to become more like those in Southern countries?



The goal of this working package is to explore the drivers of vegetation changes across different wetland types and trends in managed versus unmanaged wetlands.
We will answer the following questions:
a) What are the main environmental and anthropogenic drivers of floristic and vegetation changes in wetlands?
b) How do floristic and vegetation changes differ in managed and unmanaged wetlands?
c) What are the trends for protected and alien species?



The aim of this last working package is to consolidate all the results and develop guidelines for the conservation of wetlands based on our findings. It is based on the following questions:
a) Are current management practices effective?
b) How can wetland nature conservation policies be improved?
c) How can current trends be stopped or reversed? (if necessary)

title: Data policy
text:
Data policy

Contributor communication — All data contributors are added to the project’s mailing list and will receive periodic updates on project progress, analyses, and upcoming publications.
Data ownership — Contributors retain full ownership of their data. They are responsible for communicating with the project leader or data managers regarding permissions, use conditions, and any restrictions.
Data use and sharing — Submitted data are used exclusively for non‑commercial, academic research. No data will be shared with third parties without explicit consent from the data owners. Upon submission, contributors may choose whether their data can also be shared with the ReSurveyEurope database; if they decline, their data will be used only within WetFlorVegChange and will not be subject to ReSurveyEurope rules.
Authorship and contributions — All data contributors will be invited to become co‑authors of publications that use their data. Co‑authorship is not automatic: it requires an intellectual contribution, such as conceptual input, preparation of new data, assistance with interpretation or analysis, or writing parts of the manuscript (in accordance with the IAVS Code of Professional Ethics). Contributors who do not participate intellectually may still qualify as co‑authors if (1) they provide unpublished data from understudied European regions or vegetation types, or (2) they contribute at least 30 time series with ≥2 repeated plots for species‑poor vegetation (<20 species/plot), or 15 time series for species‑rich vegetation (>20 species/plot).

title: WetFlorVegChange
section: Floristic and Vegetation Changes in European Wetlands
text:
Floristic and Vegetation Changes in European Wetlands
Wetlands are among the most threatened ecosystems in Europe and in the World. Despite their ecological importance, our understanding of long‑term floristic and vegetation changes at the continental scale remains fragmented. Most existing studies focus on local case studies, leaving large‑scale patterns and drivers poorly understood.
WetFlorVegChange addresses this gap by building the first coordinated European network dedicated to wetland resurveys. The project brings together experts, historical data sets, and new field campaigns to assess how wetland vegetation has changed over the last century.

title: WetFlorVegChange
text:
Our Goals

Document long‑term changes in wetland flora and vegetation across Europe
Compare trends between managed and unmanaged wetlands
Identify the key drivers of changes (e.g., hydrological alteration, eutrophication, land‑use change, and climate warming)
Assess impacts on protected, rare, and alien species
Provide evidence‑based guidelines for wetland conservation and management

title: WetFlorVegChange
text:
Our Approach
We combine multiple data sources and analytical tools to build the first continental‑scale picture of wetland vegetation change:

Permanent and semi‑permanent plots and floristic resurveys from across Europe
Gap‑targeted field resurveys to revisit precisely located historical plots and fill missing regions or habitat types
Taxonomic and habitat harmonization using standardized European systems to ensure comparability across countries and decades
Repeated species‑pool analyses and vegetation‑plot time series to quantify changes in richness, composition, functional traits, and ecological indicators
GIS‑based environmental data (climate, hydrology, soils, land use) to evaluate environmental and anthropogenic drivers
Comparisons of managed vs. unmanaged wetlands to understand how conservation practices influence long‑term trends

The project will establish ReSurveyWetlands, a dedicated database for wetland vegetation resurveys, developed in close cooperation with the ReSurveyEurope initiative.

title: Related Projects and Initiatives
text:
Related Projects and Initiatives

ReSurveyEurope - the largest European database of resurvey plots, integrated with the European Vegetation Archive. It currently includes more than 120,000 plots with repeated surveys across all European Habitats.
forestREplot– a database of forest herb‑layer resurvey plots. forestREplot and ReSurveyEurope exchange European datasets when data owners provide consent.
GLORIA – the Global Observation Research Initiative in Alpine Environments. GLORIA contributes European datasets to ReSurveyEurope.
LOTVS – the Long‑Term Vegetation Sampling database. LOTVS and ReSurveyEurope share European data when data owners.
sPlot – the Global Vegetation Database. Starting with version 4.0, sPlot is collecting vegetation time‑series outside Europe and is seeking consent from ReSurveyEurope contributors to combine European datasets with global data for analyses following sPlot rules.
VegCHange – a toolbox for investigating anthropogenic changes in Swiss flora and vegetation.
EVAmap– is a mapping application for all plots included in the European Vegetation Archive and ResurveyEurope. It allows selecting plots based on geographical location, along with other criteria. It also assesses which plots have been resurveyed to assess vegetation changes over time.

title: How to contribute?
text:
How to contribute?
First, contact the project leader, Flavia Landucci (flavia.landucci@gmail.com), and express your interest in participating in this project.
You can contribute by sharing with us:
-Already existing data. Time series that are already digitized, available in literature or reports, but not stored in any existing database.
-Resurveying wetland sites. If you have good initial datasets that could be repeated within the next two years, you can conduct the resurveys yourself.
It is possible to contribute your data in two ways:
-Contribute them to the ReSurvey Europe database (https://euroveg.org/resurvey/) before October 2027 (the sooner the better). In this case, please follow all instructions on the ReSurvey webpage and notify Flavia Landucci (flavia.landucci@gmail.com) that you have contributed your data through ReSurvey Europe.
-Share them directly with our group. If, for some reason, you want to share your data only with our project and not contribute your data to ReSurvey Europe, or you do not have time to properly digitize them in a TURBOVEG database, you can contribute them directly to our data managers: Tomáš Peterka: (peterkatomasek@seznam.cz) for mires and bogs, and Zdenka Preislerová (zpreislerova@gmail.com) for all other wetland types.

title: What data are we looking for?
text:
● Permanent and (semi-)permanent plots
● Repeated surveys
● Repeated floristic species pool surveys of small wetlands (e.g., springs, ponds, pools, stream sections, etc.)
We are interested in time-series whose first survey was within the following habitat categories:

Tab.1 - List of habitats and vegetation types according to the old EUNIS classification and Annex I list of the Habitat Directive.

Tab. 2 - List of Habitats according to the new revised EUNIS Habitat classification (the revision is still in progress for the inland wetland habitats).


To ensure maximum utility and comparability, the data sets need to include:
● A complete list of vascular plants, preferably with information on abundance or abundance proxies such as cover or biomass
● Location: Geographical coordinates or detailed site descriptions.
● Location precision and, if necessary, a short description of the reasons that prevented finding the exact location.
● Survey Details: Sampling date and methodological notes (e.g., sampling surface, cover scale, inclusion/exclusion of algae and bryophytes, etc.).
● Specification of the protected area name and type (if applicable).
● Physicochemical and other additional descriptive parameters, and management types of the survey locations (if available).
● Contact. Name and contact of the data owner and data custodian
Data should be provided in Excel or Turboveg. Text formats or undigitized data are not ideal, but we will also try to accommodate them.



● Internships: If you supervise a student whose thesis relates to this subject, they can apply for an internship in our department (various mobility programs are available).
● New Resurveys: If you have good initial datasets that could be repeated within the next two years, you can conduct the resurveys yourself and contribute. In this case, contact us. We will send you a brief manual on resurveying plots for this specific project.
● If you have interesting data sets or a specific data set (published or unpublished by old authors) that you are unable to resurvey, contact us, and we can try to organize a joint fieldwork.



● Become part of a European-wide expert network on wetland ecology.
● Gain co-authorship opportunities in joint publications
● Increase the visibility of your datasets and research
● Supportthe development of evidence-based conservation guidelines for wetlands
